sounds.name: Normal heart sounds
sounds.desc: S1 ("lub", mitral + tricuspid closing) then S2 ("dub", aortic + pulmonary closing), regular, about 70 per minute. Systole (S1→S2) is shorter than diastole (S2→S1).

sounds.name: Normal heart sounds (adult)
sounds.desc: Another normal lub-dub, recorded on an electronic stethoscope. Learn this rhythm cold so the abnormal ones jump out.

sounds.name: Sinus bradycardia (athlete)
sounds.desc: Normal lub-dub but slow: 42 per minute in an elite athlete. A big, well-trained heart pumps more blood per beat, so it needs fewer beats. Normal for athletes.

sounds.name: Sinus tachycardia (after running)
sounds.desc: Fast but regular lub-dubs while recovering from a hard run. At high rates diastole shortens so much that S1 and S2 sound almost evenly spaced.

sounds.name: Atrial fibrillation (rapid)
sounds.desc: "Irregularly irregular": no pattern at all to the gaps between beats, and the loudness of S1 varies. The atria quiver instead of beating; the AV node lets impulses through randomly.

sounds.name: Premature (extra) beats
sounds.desc: A mostly regular rhythm interrupted by early beats, often followed by a pause. In a healthy teen after exercise these are usually harmless ectopic beats.

sounds.name: Innocent Still's murmur (toddler)
sounds.desc: A soft, musical, "vibratory" or twanging systolic murmur in a young child. Innocent: no heart disease. Gets softer when the child sits up.

sounds.name: Innocent flow murmur (teen)
sounds.desc: A soft systolic "whoosh" from fast blood flow through normal valves, common in fit teens. Normal S1 and S2, no symptoms.

sounds.name: Mitral valve prolapse + regurgitation
sounds.desc: A mid-systolic CLICK (the floppy mitral leaflet snapping back into the atrium) followed by a late systolic murmur as blood leaks backward.

sounds.name: Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
sounds.desc: A harsh holosystolic murmur (fills all of systole) from blood jetting through a hole between the ventricles, left to right. Small holes are often the LOUDEST.

sounds.name: Carotid bruit
sounds.desc: Not the heart: a whooshing sound over the neck artery from turbulent flow through a 70% narrowing (carotid stenosis), a stroke risk.

sounds.name: Wheeze
sounds.desc: A high-pitched musical whistle, mostly breathing OUT, from air squeezing through narrowed small airways (asthma, COPD).
sounds.artist: James Heilman, MD (noise reduction: Natural Phi)

sounds.name: Coarse crackles (pneumonia)
sounds.desc: Low-pitched bubbling/popping from fluid and pus in the airways and alveoli. Classic in pneumonia; may change after coughing.

sounds.name: Fine "velcro" crackles (pulmonary fibrosis)
sounds.desc: Fine, crisp crackles at the END of breathing in, like pulling velcro apart: stiff scarred alveoli snapping open. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

sounds.name: Stridor (croup)
sounds.desc: A harsh, high-pitched noise from a narrowed UPPER airway (larynx/trachea), loudest breathing IN. Here in a 13-month-old with croup. Stridor at rest is an emergency sign.

sounds.name: Stridor + barky cough (croup)
sounds.desc: Croup in an 11-month-old: inspiratory stridor and the seal-like barking cough from swelling below the vocal cords.

sounds.name: Whooping cough (child)
sounds.desc: Pertussis: a burst of rapid coughs, then a loud "whoop" as air rushes in through a narrowed larynx. Vaccines prevent it.

sounds.name: Whooping cough (adult)
sounds.desc: Adults often don't whoop as clearly: long coughing fits that end in retching. The "100-day cough".

sounds.name: Bonus: high-pitched bowel sounds (obstruction)
sounds.desc: Not the lungs: "tinkling" high-pitched bowel sounds over the belly in a small bowel obstruction, as the gut works against a blockage.

inst.name: Scalpel
inst.use: Makes the skin incision and cuts tissue. The blade (e.g. #10 for big cuts, #15 for small precise ones) clips onto the handle.
inst.tip: The first instrument in almost every operation.

inst.name: Mayo scissors
inst.use: Heavy scissors for cutting tough tissue like fascia, and for cutting sutures.
inst.tip: Shorter, thicker blades than Metzenbaum.

inst.name: Metzenbaum scissors
inst.use: Delicate scissors with long handles and short blades for cutting and dissecting soft tissue.
inst.tip: "Metz" = delicate; never use them on sutures.

inst.name: Hemostats (artery forceps)
inst.use: Locking clamps that squeeze a bleeding vessel shut until it can be tied or cauterized.
inst.tip: The ratchet lock keeps them closed hands-free.

inst.name: Needle holder (Mathieu)
inst.use: Grips the curved suture needle firmly for sewing tissue. Mathieu-style holders open with a squeeze-and-release spring.
inst.tip: Needle holders have short, strong jaws, often with a gold handle for tungsten carbide jaws.

inst.name: Adson forceps
inst.use: Small fine tissue forceps ("pickups") for holding skin edges while suturing.
inst.tip: Toothed versions grip skin without slipping.

inst.name: DeBakey forceps
inst.use: Long atraumatic forceps with fine grooved jaws that hold vessels and bowel without crushing them.
inst.tip: Named after heart surgeon Michael DeBakey.

inst.name: Weitlaner retractor
inst.use: Self-retaining retractor with sharp prongs that holds a small incision open by itself (ratchet).
inst.tip: Self-retaining = no assistant needed to hold it.

inst.name: Deaver retractor
inst.use: Hand-held, smoothly curved retractor for holding back organs in deep belly or chest incisions.
inst.tip: Shaped like a big question mark.

inst.name: Self-retaining retractor
inst.use: A frame retractor that locks open to hold a large incision apart for the whole operation.
inst.tip: Frees up the assistant's hands.

inst.name: Yankauer suction tip
inst.use: Rigid suction tip for clearing blood and fluid from the surgical field or the mouth and throat.
inst.tip: The bulbous tip with side holes avoids sucking onto tissue.

inst.name: Kerrison rongeurs
inst.use: Bone punches that bite small pieces of bone with an upward cut. Workhorse of spine surgery for widening the spinal canal.
inst.tip: Comes in sizes like 2 mm and 3 mm bite.

inst.name: Bone rongeur
inst.use: Heavy plier-like instrument with a cupped tip that gouges and nibbles away bone.
inst.tip: "Rongeur" is French for rodent: it nibbles.

inst.name: Periosteal elevator
inst.use: Scrapes the periosteum (the tough skin of bone) off the bone surface so the bone can be exposed.
inst.tip: In neurosurgery, used to peel tissue off the skull.

inst.name: Osteotome
inst.use: A chisel used with a mallet to cut or shape bone.
inst.tip: An osteotome is bevelled on both sides; a chisel on one.

inst.name: Skin stapler
inst.use: Closes skin incisions fast with metal staples, removed later with a staple remover.
inst.tip: Quicker than suturing for long incisions (and scalp closure).

inst.name: Tongue depressor
inst.use: Wooden blade that holds the tongue down to see the throat.
inst.tip: Also used to test the gag reflex (CN IX and X).

inst.name: Laryngoscope
inst.use: Lighted blade that lifts the tongue and epiglottis to see the vocal cords and place a breathing tube (intubation).
inst.tip: Curved = Macintosh blade; straight = Miller.

inst.name: Otoscope
inst.use: Lighted magnifier with a cone tip for looking at the ear canal and eardrum.
inst.tip: Red bulging eardrum = middle ear infection.

inst.name: Reflex hammer (tomahawk)
inst.use: Rubber hammer for tapping tendons to test deep tendon reflexes.
inst.tip: Biceps C5–6, triceps C7, knee L3–4, ankle S1.

inst.name: Tuning fork (Rydel-Seiffer)
inst.use: Vibrating fork for testing vibration sense (peripheral nerves) and hearing (Rinne and Weber tests).
inst.tip: The sliding weights let you grade vibration sense from 0 to 8.

inst.name: Ophthalmoscope
inst.use: Lighted scope with lenses for looking through the pupil at the retina and optic disc.
inst.tip: A swollen optic disc (papilledema) means raised pressure inside the skull.

derm.name: Atopic dermatitis (eczema)
derm.desc: Dry, itchy, red, scaly patches, often in the elbow and knee creases in kids. A leaky skin barrier plus allergic (type 2) inflammation; linked to asthma and hay fever (the "atopic triad").

derm.name: Plaque psoriasis
derm.desc: Well-defined red plaques with thick silvery-white scale on the outer elbows, knees and scalp. Autoimmune: T cells (IL-17/IL-23) speed up skin cell turnover about 10×.

derm.name: Urticaria (hives)
derm.desc: Raised, itchy wheals that move around and each fade within 24 hours. Mast cells release histamine, so H1 antihistamines help.

derm.name: Chickenpox (varicella)
derm.desc: Itchy spots in different stages at once: red papules, clear blisters ("dewdrops on a rose petal") and crusts, starting on the trunk and face. Varicella-zoster virus; vaccine-preventable.

derm.name: Measles rash
derm.desc: Blotchy red maculopapular rash that starts at the hairline and spreads down, after fever, cough, runny nose and conjunctivitis. Koplik spots in the mouth come first. Vaccine-preventable.
derm.artist: CDC / National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases

derm.name: Shingles (herpes zoster), forehead
derm.desc: Painful blisters in ONE dermatome that stop at the midline: chickenpox virus reactivating from a sensory ganglion. Here the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which can threaten the eye.

derm.name: Impetigo
derm.desc: "Honey-coloured" golden crusts, often around the nose and mouth or on limbs. Superficial bacterial infection (Staph aureus or Strep pyogenes); very contagious.

derm.name: Tinea corporis (ringworm)
derm.desc: A ring-shaped red patch with a scaly raised edge and clearing centre. A fungus (dermatophyte), not a worm. Treated with antifungals.

derm.name: Acne vulgaris (nodular)
derm.desc: Blackheads, whiteheads, red papules and pustules, here with deeper nodules. Blocked hair follicles + oil + Cutibacterium acnes + inflammation.

derm.name: Cellulitis
derm.desc: Spreading, hot, red, swollen, tender skin with a blurry edge, often on a lower leg. Bacterial infection of the deeper skin (usually Strep or Staph). Needs antibiotics.

derm.name: Erythema migrans (Lyme disease)
derm.desc: An expanding red "bull's-eye" rash at a tick bite, days to weeks later. Borrelia burgdorferi. Untreated Lyme can cause facial nerve palsy and meningitis.

derm.name: Hand, foot and mouth disease
derm.desc: Small oval blisters on palms, soles and inside the mouth, usually in young kids. Coxsackievirus (enterovirus).

derm.name: Scarlet fever tongue
derm.desc: A red "raspberry/strawberry" tongue, with a sandpaper-feel rash and sore throat. Group A Strep toxin. Treated with antibiotics.

derm.name: Vitiligo
derm.desc: Sharp-edged completely white patches where melanocytes have been destroyed by the immune system. Not contagious.

derm.name: Allergic contact dermatitis (poison ivy)
derm.desc: Itchy red rash with blisters, often in STREAKS where the plant brushed the skin. A type IV (delayed T-cell) reaction to urushiol oil.

derm.name: Purpura / petechiae
derm.desc: Red-purple spots that DON'T fade when pressed (glass test): bleeding into the skin. With fever, think meningococcal sepsis: emergency.

derm.name: Pityriasis rosea
derm.desc: Starts with one larger "herald patch", then many oval pink patches along skin lines on the back in a "Christmas tree" pattern. Probably viral; fades in 6–8 weeks.

derm.name: Melanoma
derm.desc: A mole that's Asymmetric, with irregular Borders, multiple Colours, Diameter over 6 mm and Evolving (ABCDE). The deadliest skin cancer, from melanocytes.

derm.name: Café-au-lait spot
derm.desc: Flat, light-brown "coffee with milk" patch. Six or more (over 5 mm in kids) suggests neurofibromatosis type 1, a nerve-tumour syndrome.
derm.artist: Jyothi Idiculla, Shine Pakalomattom, Anasuya Desai, Babu Philip

derm.name: Port-wine stain
derm.desc: A flat pink-purple birthmark from dilated capillaries, present at birth. On the forehead/upper face (V1 area) it can go with Sturge-Weber syndrome (brain vessel malformation, seizures).

derm.name: Erythema multiforme (target lesions)
derm.desc: "Target" spots with a dark centre, pale ring and red outer ring, often on hands and arms. Most often triggered by herpes simplex (cold sores) or a medicine.

derm.name: Rosacea
derm.desc: Facial flushing, redness and visible small vessels on cheeks and nose, sometimes with bumps but NO blackheads (unlike acne). Common in adults.
derm.artist: M. Sand, D. Sand, C. Thrandorf, V. Paech, P. Altmeyer, F. G. Bechara

histo.name: Skeletal muscle
histo.desc: Long cylindrical fibres with STRIATIONS (stripes) and many nuclei pushed to the edge of each cell. Voluntary muscle.
histo.artist: Department of Histology, Jagiellonian University Medical College

histo.name: Smooth muscle
histo.desc: Spindle-shaped cells with ONE central cigar-shaped nucleus and no stripes. In gut, vessels and airways; involuntary.

histo.name: Cardiac muscle (with Purkinje fibres)
histo.desc: Branching striated cells with one central nucleus, joined by intercalated discs. The paler, bigger cells are Purkinje fibres that conduct the heartbeat signal fast.

histo.name: Hyaline (articular) cartilage
histo.desc: Chondrocytes sitting in little holes (lacunae), often in rows or pairs, in a smooth glassy matrix. No blood vessels, so it heals poorly.
histo.artist: Bautista CA, Park HJ, Mazur CM, Aaron RK, Bilgen B

histo.name: Compact bone (ground section)
histo.desc: Concentric rings (lamellae) around a central Haversian canal = an osteon. The dark dots are lacunae where osteocytes live.
histo.artist: Department of Histology, Jagiellonian University Medical College

histo.name: Spongy (trabecular) bone
histo.desc: A lattice of thin pink bone struts (trabeculae) with bone marrow in the spaces between. Found inside vertebrae and the ends of long bones.
histo.artist: Department of Histology, Jagiellonian University Medical College

histo.name: Glomerulus (kidney)
histo.desc: A ball of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule where blood is filtered into urine. PAS stain highlights basement membranes.

histo.name: Lung alveoli
histo.desc: A lacy network of very thin-walled air sacs around a small airway. The thin walls let oxygen and CO2 diffuse quickly.

histo.name: Thyroid follicles
histo.desc: Round follicles lined by one layer of cells, filled with pink colloid (stored thyroglobulin, the raw material for thyroid hormone).

histo.name: Motor neuron (spinal cord)
histo.desc: A huge multipolar neuron with a big round nucleus, prominent nucleolus and several processes. Lives in the anterior horn and drives skeletal muscle.
histo.artist: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

histo.name: Cerebellar cortex (Purkinje cells)
histo.desc: A row of big flask-shaped Purkinje neurons between the outer molecular layer and the dense granular layer. The cerebellum's only output neurons.

histo.name: Peripheral nerve
histo.desc: Bundles of axons wrapped in myelin with Schwann-cell nuclei, packaged in connective tissue sheaths (endo-, peri-, epineurium).
histo.artist: Department of Histology, Jagiellonian University Medical College

histo.name: Neutrophil (blood smear)
histo.desc: A white blood cell with a nucleus in 3–5 lobes and pale cytoplasm, among pink red blood cells with no nuclei. First responder to bacteria.

histo.name: Trachea epithelium
histo.desc: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells (mucus). The cilia sweep mucus up and out: the mucociliary escalator.

histo.name: Esophagus epithelium
histo.desc: Stratified squamous epithelium (many layers, flat on top, NOT keratinized) that resists the friction of swallowed food.

histo.name: Pancreatic islet
histo.desc: A pale island of endocrine cells (beta cells make insulin, alpha cells glucagon) surrounded by darker exocrine acini that make digestive enzymes.
histo.artist: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

histo.name: Adipose tissue (fat)
histo.desc: Big empty-looking round cells: the fat droplet dissolves during processing, leaving a thin rim and a squashed nucleus at the edge ("signet ring").
histo.artist: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

histo.name: Muscular artery (elastic stain)
histo.desc: Thick wall of smooth muscle with wavy black internal and external elastic laminae. Arteries have thicker walls and rounder lumens than veins.

histo.name: Stomach mucosa
histo.desc: Gastric pits leading into tubular glands. Fundic glands hold parietal cells (acid, intrinsic factor) and chief cells (pepsinogen).

histo.name: Lymph node
histo.desc: Outer cortex with round follicles (B cells), deeper paracortex (T cells) and medulla, with a capsule and subcapsular sinus where lymph enters.

histo.name: Liver
histo.desc: Plates (cords) of hepatocytes radiating from central veins, with sinusoids between them. Arranged in hexagonal lobules with portal triads at the corners.
histo.artist: Department of Histology, Jagiellonian University Medical College
